name: yApoptosis
descriptions: yeast apoptosis database
usage_summaries: Researchers cross-referenced 51 apoptosis-related yeast genes with differential-expression data from hydrogen-peroxide oxidative-stress studies. They assessed transcriptional changes across strains, peroxide concentrations and exposure times.
usage_patterns: Retrieved 51 apoptosis-related yeast genes, which were cross-referenced with differential-expression data from H2O2-induced oxidative-stress studies to assess transcriptional changes across strains, peroxide concentrations, and exposure times.

name: PhenomicDB
descriptions: PhenomicDB is a multi-species genotype/phenotype database,integrating public genotype/phenotype data from a wide range of modelorganisms and Homo sapiens. Genotype and phenotype descriptions areobtained from Entrez Gene, OMIM, wormbase, flybase, and many othercollections. Phenotypes cover e.g. mutant screens, k.o. mice, or RNAinterference. In addition, clinical descriptions and naturally occurringmutants are also available. As phenotypes are linked to genes whichthemselves are grouped according to orthology, users can easily comparephenotypes of a gene of interest over a wide range of organisms. Likewise,users can discover  genes involved in phenotypes as diverse as neural tubedefects, Alzheimer disease, apoptosis, or polyploidy.
usage_summaries: PhenomicDB provided multispecies phenotype descriptions for text-based phenoclustering and gene-function analyses. Researchers grouped genes by phenotypic similarity and evaluated or predicted functions using Gene Ontology, protein–protein interactions and phenocopies. They also retrieved yeast-expressed gene annotations and concatenated each gene’s textual phenotypes for downstream analysis.

Researchers searched PhenomicDB for PCOS-related genes and proteins when building PCOSBase. They also combined its RNAi phenotype experiments with WormBase data and organised them into hierarchical phenotype categories in CMGSDB.
usage_patterns: Provided multispecies phenotype descriptions for text-based phenoclustering, grouping genes by phenotypic similarity and evaluating or predicting gene function using Gene Ontology, protein–protein interactions, and phenocopies.
Was queried to retrieve phenotype annotations for yeast-expressed genes, with each gene’s textual phenotypes concatenated into a document for downstream analysis.
Was searched alongside other disease-associated databases to collect PCOS-related genes and proteins for PCOSBase.
Supplied additional RNAi phenotype experiments that were combined with WormBase data and organized into hierarchical phenotype categories in CMGSDB.

name: MorpheusML
descriptions: Multicellular spatial models incl. cell behaviors like motility, division and apoptosis as well as cell and tissue mechanics have become an essential tool in quantitative biology and multiple simulation frameworks coexist. The MultiCellML consortium within COMBINE develops model declaration languages and conversion libraries to foster software interoperability and simulation reproducibility. Building on the community‘s practical experiences with multiple simulators for the Cellular Potts Model, we developed MorpheusML as a first step towards MultiCellML and as a prototype standard to test the software infrastructure for sharing multicellular models across simulators. MorpheusML models are already shared at BioModels and other model repositories and they can be loaded, simulated and saved in the simulators Artistoo and Morpheus. Extensions to further simulation frameworks are in progress.

name: HomoMINT
descriptions: <<<!!!<<< This repository is no longer available. >>>!!!>>>
usage_summaries: Researchers merged HomoMINT interactions with experimental and orthology-mapped sources to build human protein-interaction networks. These networks supported disease-gene prioritisation, biological modules, pathway and tissue-specific analyses, while retained experimental-species information extended coverage with interologs, interactions inferred through orthologous proteins.

Method developers used HomoMINT interaction pairs as experimentally supported reference data. They benchmarked protein-interaction prediction algorithms, assessed network quality, and compared the coverage or novelty of interaction resources.
usage_patterns: HomoMINT interactions were merged with other experimentally supported or orthology-mapped PPI sources to construct human interaction networks for disease-gene prioritization, disease similarity, susceptibility neighborhoods, cancer modules, apoptosis, phosphatase, and other biological-network analyses.

HomoMINT/MINT interactions supplied physical or first-degree protein relationships for pathway, tissue-specific, host–pathogen, disease-platform, proteomic, phosphoproteomic, and functional-enrichment analyses.

HomoMINT’s orthology-based interactions and retained experimental-species information were used to extend human PPI coverage with interologs and to support confidence scoring or comparison of human interaction maps.

HomoMINT interaction pairs were used as experimentally supported reference or gold-standard data to benchmark PPI-prediction algorithms, assess network quality, and compare interaction-resource coverage or novelty.

name: Human Unidentified Gene-Encoded large proteins database
descriptions: Database of the human cDNA project at the Kazusa DNA Research Institute, covering various sets of large human proteins of hitherto unidentified functions.

HUGE is a database for human large proteins newly identified in the Kazusa cDNA project, the aim of which is to predict the primary structure of proteins from the sequences of human large cDNAs (>4 kb).
usage_summaries: Researchers used full-length human cDNAs and reliable brain splice junctions to study alternative splicing, annotate transcripts and model protein domains. Kazusa HUGE sequences also supported protein-fragment solubility experiments and primer design for CAPON transcript measurement in postmortem prefrontal cortex.

Researchers investigated KIAA0100 through sequence analysis and CRISPR/Cas9 downregulation in U937 cells. They expressed residues 1557–2234, generated a monoclonal antibody and detected endogenous KIAA0100 protein products.
Researchers used KIF5B, KIF1B and KIF1C cDNA constructs from Kazusa image clones for expression in HeLa cells during studies of kinesin-driven secretory-vesicle transport.
usage_patterns: Used reliable splice junctions from long human brain cDNAs to test how alternative splicing relates to protein structure, finding that splice events avoid SCOP-domain interiors and cluster at domain boundaries.

Provided KIAA0100 as the previously uncharacterized human gene investigated through sequence analysis and CRISPR/Cas9 downregulation in U937 leukemia cells, supporting an anti-apoptotic role in acute monocytic leukemia.
Provided the KIAA0100 sequence used to express residues 1557–2234, generate a monoclonal antibody, and detect endogenous protein products in U937 cells.

Contributed validated full-length cDNAs to the H-Invitational annotation pipeline, where sequences were checked for quality, genome identity, orientation, chimerism, truncation, and cross-species contamination before H-InvDB construction.
Supplied Kazusa HUGE protein sequences for estimating a probabilistic model that predicted domains and guided experimental testing of large-scale protein fragments for solubility.
Provided the CAPON clone KIAA0464 for primer design to quantify full-length CAPON transcripts in postmortem dorsolateral prefrontal cortex from schizophrenia, bipolar-disorder, and control subjects.
Supplied human KIF5B, KIF1B, and KIF1C cDNA constructs from Kazusa image clones for expression in HeLa cells during experiments on kinesin-driven secretory-vesicle transport.

name: FAIRDOMHub
descriptions: Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Reusable Data, Operating procedures and Models

The FAIRDOMHub is a publicly available repository managed and supported by the FAIRDOM consortium (https://fair-dom.org/).
It's build using the FAIRDOM-SEEK software (http://fairdomseek.org), an open source web platform for storing, sharing and publishing research assets of biology projects. The assets include FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Reusable) Data, Operating procedures and Models. 
FAIRDOMHub enables researchers to organize, share and publish data, models and protocols, interlink them in the context of the biology investigations that produced them, and to interrogate them via API interfaces. By using the FAIRDOMHub, researchers can achieve more effective exchange with geographically distributed collaborators during projects, ensure results are sustained and preserved and generate reproducible publications that adhere to the FAIR guiding principles of data stewardship. FAIRDOMHub includes special support for the Systems Biology community.

The FAIRDOMHub is a web-accessible registry for storing, sharing and publishing research assets of biology projects. The assets include FAIR Data, Operating procedures and Models. 
FAIRDOMHub enables researchers to organize, share and publish data, models and protocols, interlink them in the context of the biology investigations that produced them, and to interrogate them via API interfaces. FAIRDOMHub includes special support for the Systems Biology community.
It is based on the FAIRDOM-SEEK open source software (https://seek4science.org//) and is managed by the FAIRDOM consortium (https://fair-dom.org).
usage_summaries: FAIRDOMHub published and archived study data, models, workflows, metadata, analysis outputs and project records, including versioned omics, sequencing, assembly and disease-map materials.
Teams used FAIRDOMHub to stage, manage, validate and FAIRify metadata before analysis, database import, publication or migration.

Researchers retrieved, visualised and reused hosted models and assay resources for computational analyses, while linking contributors, licences, data and resources for disease-map dissemination and FAIRness assessment.
usage_patterns: Used to publish or archive study data, models, workflows, metadata, analysis outputs, and supporting project records, including kinetic models, sequencing and assembly data, omics resources, disease-map artifacts, reproducibility materials, and versioned data files.

Used as a staging, metadata-management, validation, or FAIRification environment before downstream analysis, database import, publication, or migration; examples include MIAPPE-compatible wheat data, consulting outputs, internal AGENT data, HCS metadata, and MIFE/RDF metadata workflows.

Used to retrieve, visualize, or reuse hosted models and assay resources in computational analysis, including C19DMap apoptosis models for multiscale SARS-CoV-2 simulations, Atlantic-cod metabolic-model gap filling, and linked assay/model records for pathway kinetic modelling.

Used to connect contributors, project metadata, licensing, data, and computational resources for disease-map dissemination and FAIRness assessment, including the COVID-19 Disease Map and Parkinson’s Disease Map infrastructure.

name: Autophagy Database
descriptions: Database that provides basic, up-to-date information on relevant literature, and a list of autophagy-related proteins and their homologs. From the database, the user can search for proteins by keywords or sequences to obtain a wealth of data including functional and structural information and find possible functional homologs of proteins whose functions have been demonstrated in other species.
Proteins involved in self-digestion of eukaryotic cells

The goal of the Autophagy Database is to provide up-to-date relevant information including protein structure data to researchers of autophagy, and to disseminate important findings to a wider audience so that their ramifications can be appreciated. For this purpose, we strive to make the database to contain as much pertinent information as possible and to make the contents freely available in a user-friendly format.
usage_summaries: Autophagy-related gene sets were intersected with molecular data to identify relevant differentially expressed genes, pathways and hubs, and supported enrichment, prognostic, risk-score, drug-resistance and immunotherapy analyses across cancer and other disease models.

The database annotated proteins for autophagy involvement in proteomic and mammalian stress-granule catalogues, and served independently when comparing Gene Ontology autophagy-annotation coverage with other sources.

Its interaction and protein records contributed to integrated autophagy and programmed-cell-death resources, while joint mining with other autophagy resources identified experimentally supported autophagy-modulating drugs.
usage_patterns: Supplied autophagy-related gene sets that were intersected with disease- or treatment-associated molecular data to identify autophagy-related differentially expressed genes, pathways, or hubs in ovarian clear cell carcinoma xenografts, silicosis, Kaiso-depleted cells, mouse liver, periodontitis, septic heart, osteoporosis, oral cancer, cartilage injury, FTD, and cardiovascular disease.

Supplied or helped curate autophagy gene sets for enrichment, signature, prognostic, risk-score, drug-resistance, and immunotherapy analyses across pan-cancer, bladder cancer, colorectal cancer TIC cultures under hypoxia, premature ovarian insufficiency, Alzheimer’s disease postmortem cohorts, osteosarcoma, ovarian cancer, esophageal squamous cell carcinoma, and multi-tumor cohorts.
Annotated proteins according to autophagy involvement in a rotenone/Yashtimadhu choorna proteomics analysis and in a curated catalogue of mammalian stress-granule components.

Contributed autophagy interaction or protein records to integrated resources: AutophagyNet, HAMdb, and a broader programmed-cell-death protein database, with records subsequently curated or checked against literature.
Was mined with other autophagy-focused resources to identify drugs with direct experimental evidence for activating, inhibiting, or otherwise modulating autophagy.
Was used as an independent resource when comparing the coverage of Gene Ontology autophagy annotations with other annotation sources.

name: piSite
descriptions: Database of Protein Interaction Sites using multiple binding states in PDB
usage_summaries: piSite supplied protein sequences and residue-level interaction annotations for assembling and evaluating protein–protein interaction-site predictors and benchmarks. Researchers also mapped these interface residues or predicted regions onto variants and modelled Rab11A and Rab23 structures to develop variant-prediction features and compare interaction-residue calls.

Researchers used piSite bound-state sites and partner annotations to compare native interfaces with simulated contacts, binding-state multiplicity, residue flexibility and solvent accessibility. It also supported structure-based functional investigation, including similarity to apoptosis proteins and sites linked with canonical or moonlighting functions.
piSite provided a protein subset for testing whether structural alphabets represent flexibility and conformational variation across balanced SCOP classes and fold representations.
usage_patterns: Supplied protein sequences and residue-level interaction sites for constructing, refreshing, training, validating, or testing protein–protein interaction-site prediction datasets and models, including ProSiteHunter, Seq-InSite, PPI-Surfer, and the Dset_500 benchmark.

Provided structural interface residues or predicted interaction regions for mapping nonsynonymous variants, building features for disease-associated variant prediction, and comparing predicted interaction residues in modeled Rab11A and Rab23 structures.

Provided bound-state structural binding sites and partner annotations for comparing native interfaces with simulated contacts, evaluating binding-state multiplicity and residue flexibility, and testing whether solvent accessibility distinguishes structural and binding residues.

Supported structure-based investigation of protein functions by identifying structural similarity to apoptosis proteins and mapping structural or functional sites associated with canonical and moonlighting functions.
Supplied a protein subset for testing whether structural alphabets encode flexibility and conformational variability across balanced SCOP classes and fold representations.

name: IPD-ESTDAB
descriptions: The Immuno Polymorphism Database (IPD) is a set of specialist databases related to the study of polymorphic genes in the immune system. IPD currently consists of four databases: IPD-KIR, contains the allelic sequences of Killer-cell Immunoglobulin-like Receptors, IPD-MHC, is a database of sequences of the major histocompatibility complex of different species; IPD-HPA, alloantigens expressed only on platelets; and IPD-ESTAB, which provides access to the European Searchable Tumour Cell-Line Database, a cell bank of immunologically characterised melanoma cell lines.IPD-ESTDAB is a database of immunologically characterised melanoma cell lines. The database works in conjunction with the European Searchable Tumour Cell Line Database (ESTDAB) cell bank, which is housed in TÜbingen, Germany and provides immunologically characterised tumour cells. The IPD-ESTDAB section of the website provides an online search facility for cells stored in this cell bank. This enables investigators to identify cells possessing specific parameters important for studies of immunity, immunogenetics, gene expression, metastasis, response to chemotherapy, and other tumour biological experimentation. The search tool allows for searches based on a single parameter, or clusters of parameters on over 250 different markers for each cell. The detailed reports produced can be then be used to identify cells of interest, which can then be obtained from the cell bank.
usage_summaries: IPD-ESTDAB melanoma lines were used to examine HLA class I and II expression, antigen processing, IFN-γ responses and mechanisms of melanoma immune escape.
The lines also served as targets for tumour-reactive T-cell, ROR1 antibody and low-oxygen growth, viability and heat-shock-protein experiments.
usage_patterns: Used ESTDAB melanoma cell lines to measure constitutive and IFN-γ-induced HLA class II expression and relate expression patterns to CIITA promoter variation.

Used ESTDAB melanoma cell lines to characterize HLA class I surface-expression alterations, including loss or down-regulation associated with LOH, haplotype loss, β2-microglobulin mutation, or regulatory effects.
Used selected ESTDAB melanoma lines as targets in RhoC-specific cytotoxic-T-cell assays to test HLA-A3-restricted tumor recognition and killing.
Used ESTDAB melanoma lines with differing antigen-processing machinery or TAP1/HLA-I profiles to investigate miRNA regulation of TAP1, HLA-I expression, and melanoma immune escape.
Used ESTDAB melanoma lines as HLA-A0201-positive or negative targets to evaluate antigen-presenting scaffolds for selective expansion of tumor-reactive T cells in adoptive-cell-therapy research.
Used ESTDAB melanoma lines to investigate cell-line-specific resistance to IFN-γ-induced HLA class I expression and the underlying STAT-1 or IRF-1-related mechanisms.
Used ESTDAB melanoma lines to assess growth, viability, and heat-shock-protein responses under physiologic low-oxygen conditions.
Used immunologically characterized ESTDAB melanoma lines to measure ROR1 expression and test antibody-mediated cytotoxicity, apoptosis, and effects of ROR1 silencing.

name: UniHI
descriptions: Systematic mapping of protein-protein interactions (PPIs) has become a central task of functional genomics. To map the human interactome, several strategies have recently been pursued. The generated interaction datasets are valuable resources for scientists in biology and medicine. However, comparison reveals limited overlap between different interaction networks. This divergence obstructs usability, as researchers have to interrogate numerous heterogeneous datasets to identify potential interaction partners for proteins of interest. To facilitate direct access through a single entry gate, we have started to integrate currently available human protein interaction data in an easily accessible online database, called UniHI (Unified Human Interactome).UniHI provides researchers with a flexible integrated tool for the exploration of the human interactome. It enables the assembly of comprehensive lists of protein interactions and flexible network-orientated searching. Network structures can be identified which would not be detectable if single maps were analyzed separately. For highly targeted search, UniHI offers several tools to specify the displayed interactions. Also, scores for quality assessment are given based on co-annotation and co-expression of the interacting proteins. Various hyperlinks to other databases facilitate users to follow-up results retrieved in UniHI.
usage_summaries: Researchers used UniHI interaction networks after normalising identifiers, filtering records or merging them with other sources. They combined these networks with cell, tissue, phenotype and expression data to construct context-specific interaction networks.

Researchers used UniHI interactions as candidate or supporting links in disease, cancer, signalling and drug-target studies. They also used it to retrieve experimentally verified interactions and compare PPI database coverage, network-analysis functions and web-resource usability.
Researchers used UniHI gene annotations and network-connectivity information in downstream resources that scored enhancer relatedness or annotated stem-cell networks.
usage_patterns: Supplied large human molecular-interaction networks that were identifier-normalized, filtered, merged with other sources, or combined with cell-, tissue-, phenotype-, and expression-specific data to construct interaction networks.

Provided candidate or supporting interactions for disease and cancer mechanism studies, including SETDB1–p21 regulation, prostate-cancer gene pairs, DLL1/CD117 signalling networks, ERβ–AGO2 comparisons, Huntington’s-disease UPR/apoptosis links, and integrin drug-target analyses.
Served as a human PPI resource for comparing database coverage, experimentally verified interaction retrieval, network-analysis functionality, and web-resource usability.
Supplied gene annotation or network-connectivity information for downstream resources that scored enhancer relatedness or annotated stem-cell networks.

name: HRTBLDb
descriptions: The Hormone Receptor Target Binding Loci, HRTBLDb database contains hormone receptor binding regions (binding loci) from in vivo ChIP-based high-throughput experiments as well as in silico, computationally predicted, binding motifs and cis-regulatory modules for the co-occurring transcription factor binding motifs, which are within a binding locus. It also contains individual binding sites whose regulatory action has been verified by in vitro experiments.
usage_summaries: Researchers used oestrogen-receptor and androgen-receptor binding-site records as enhancer annotations when examining chromatin signatures at distal regulatory regions. They mapped promoter-pattern regions against these sites, including 120 unmapped regions that overlapped oestrogen-receptor sites.

Researchers used R1881-treated LNCaP-cell records to locate an androgen-receptor-occupied region 81 kb downstream of AIFM2. They treated AIFM2 as a putative androgen-regulated apoptosis-gene target pending experimental confirmation.
usage_patterns: Used ER and AR binding-site records as enhancer annotations to test whether promoter-like chromatin signatures also occur at distal regulatory regions; 120 unmapped promoter-pattern regions overlapped ER sites and none overlapped AR sites after mapping.

Used R1881-treated LNCaP-cell records to locate an AR-occupied region 81 kb downstream of AIFM2, supporting AIFM2 as a putative androgen-regulated apoptosis-gene target pending experimental confirmation.
tags: nucleic acid sites, features and motifs

name: lncHUB2
descriptions: Aggregated and inferred knowledge about human and mouse lncRNAs.
usage_patterns: In breast-cancer research, lncHUB2 was combined with other resources to predict Nkx2-2as functional interactions and direct attention to Wnt/β-catenin signaling as a possible progression mechanism.

For post hoc analysis of lncRNAs identified by lncAPNet, lncHUB2 used normalized ARCHS4 expression profiles and UMAP to visualize lncRNA relationships, including clustering newly identified CLL-associated lncRNAs with reported ones.

In diabetic ischemic heart disease, lncHUB2 was used to functionally analyze dysregulated left-ventricular lncRNAs through co-expression, tissue/cell-line expression, pathway, function, and localization information, guiding validation of Gm19522 and Gm8075.

In colorectal-cancer ceRNA-network construction, lncHUB co-expression correlations were used to predict candidate lncRNA functions and enrichments, implicating specific lncRNAs in immune, oxidative-stress, WNT, inflammatory, epithelial, and extracellular-matrix processes.

In evaluating GeneRAIN gene embeddings learned from ARCHS4 bulk RNA-seq, lncHUB co-expression annotations were used as biological attribute groups to test whether embeddings captured gene-group structure.

In Brucella abortus-infected macrophages, lncHUB2 supplied lncRNA-correlated genes that were intersected with infection-associated differentially expressed genes to construct immune-interaction networks for five immunomodulatory lncRNAs.

In diabetic-cardiomyopathy systems biology, lncHUB2/lncHUB co-expression predictions were combined with disease and target-gene networks to identify candidate regulatory lncRNAs and their ceRNA-linked inflammatory, metabolic, apoptotic, PI3K-Akt, IL-17, mitochondrial, and oxidative-phosphorylation associations.

name: EKPD
descriptions: The reversible phosphorylation of proteins is one of the most important post-translational modifications, which is involved in varieties of cellular processes and plays a critical role in activation, inactivation and regulation of proteins. Two types of enzymes, known as protein kinase and protein phosphatase, are responsible for this reversible reaction and almost constitute about 2~4% of the genes in a typical eukaryotic genome (Moorhead et al., 2009). Protein kinase is a type of well understood enzyme which modifies other proteins by chemically adding phosphate groups to them (phosphorylation). Protein kinases have been found to be involved in varieties of cellular processes, including metabolism (Viollet and Andreelli 2011), transcription, cell cycle progression (Moniz et al., 2011), cytoskeleton rearrangement and cell movement (Huang et al., 2009), cell apoptosis (Wang, 2000), and differentiation (Taylor et al., 2011). Contrary to phosphorylation, dephosphorylation is catalyzed by protein phosphatase through a way of removing a phosphate group from its substrate. Protein phosphatases contain two groups, PSP and PTP, which are responsible for the ser/thr dephosphorylation and tyr dephosphorylation respectively. Like protein kinases, protein phosphatases also play an important role in a lot of cellular processes, including proliferation (Zhang et al., 2012), differentiation, cell adhesion (Bessette et al., 2008), motility and cell death (Gallego et al., 2005). As the critical roles in biological processes, abnormal level of phosphorylation or dephosphorylation is implicated in diseases, such as myotonic muscular dystrophy, hirschsprungis disease, leprechaunism, diabetes and so on (Cohen, 2001). Although the studies on phosphorylation and dephosphorylation last for a long time, and many related resources have been developed, however, a comprehensive classification of all protein kinases and protein phosphatases and how many potential two types of enzymes exist in usual and rare species still remains not to be available. In this work, we have collected 347 protein phosphatase data from literatures, integrated and curated five protein kinase complements of H. sapiens, M. musculus, D. melanogaster, C. elegans and S. cerevisiae from KinBase with a total number of 1,855. The data are further classified into 10 groups and 33 families for protein phosphatase, 10 groups and 149 families for protein kinase, respectively. The protein kinase and protein phosphatase identification in 84 eukaryotic species is based on the Hidden Markov Model (HMM) of their catalytic domains (Eddy, 1998). Currently, the Eukaryotic Kinase and Phosphatase Database -- EKPD is the most comprehensive resource to get protein kinases and protein phosphatases information in eukaryotic organisms.
usage_patterns: Supplied kinase and phosphatase classifications, families, protein identities, or sequences for enzyme annotation and candidate discovery, including kinase/phosphatase prediction, comparison of Arabidopsis kinase classifications, and use of Arabidopsis PP2C references or PP2C domains to identify PP2C genes in polyploid sugarcane and barley pan-genomes.

Provided kinase-class information for phosphoproteomics interpretation: EKPD kinase groups, including the 89-member CDPK/SnRK family within CAMK, were used to enrich rhythmic phosphopeptides and nominate kinases associated with dawn-peaking phosphorylation; human kinase names were also used to retrieve activity-site evidence for quantitative kinase-activity profiling.
Served as a source or baseline for integrating rice protein-kinase/phosphatase classifications into IC4R and for developing and benchmarking the expanded iEKPD 2.0 resource.

Was used in phosphatase-resource comparison and manual cross-checking, including identifying STS-1 as an additional phosphatase and supporting its classification as a family-8 enzyme with tyrosine-phosphatase activity.

name: DiSignAtlas
descriptions: Atlas of human and mouse disease signatures based on bulk and single-cell transcriptomics.
DiSignAtlas: an atlas of human and mouse disease signatures based on bulk and single-cell transcriptomics
usage_summaries: DiSignAtlas provided disease-expression data for translational and signalling-network analyses. Researchers compared murine SLE-model genes with human disease signatures, assessed expression of genes linked to neurological-network factors, built disease-specific graphs across nine diseases and tested UBE2S expression in melanoma and adjacent-normal datasets.
Researchers used DiSignAtlas as a manually curated benchmark to evaluate RummaGEO disease and perturbation sample partitions, including complex time-series studies.
usage_patterns: Tested whether 27 TRIF- and IRF3-dependent genes from an induced murine SLE model matched human disease signatures, identifying enrichment for autoimmune and viral immune-response datasets, especially human SLE datasets.

Served as the manually curated benchmark for evaluating RummaGEO disease/perturbation sample partitions with the Adjusted Rand Index, including assessment of disagreements in complex time-series studies.

Supplied neurological-disease transcriptomic datasets attached to signaling-network analyses to assess differential expression of genes linked to identified factors, including apoptosis and TUBA-related factors.

Supplied case/control gene-expression data for constructing disease-specific graphs in ID-GBA across nine diseases, including ulcerative colitis, invasive breast carcinoma, asthma, lung adenocarcinoma, dilated cardiomyopathy, arthritis, psoriasis, COPD, and type 2 diabetes.
Provided melanoma and adjacent-normal expression datasets for testing UBE2S expression in skin cutaneous melanoma, showing elevated expression in GSE101685 and GSE6764.

name: COLT-Cancer
descriptions: Collection of shRNA dropout signatures profiles, covering ~16000 human genes, and derived from more than 70 Pancreatic, Ovarian and Breast human cancer cell-lines using a microarray detection platform.
Essential gene profiles in human cancer cell lines
usage_patterns: Used genome-wide pooled-shRNA essentiality profiles from cancer cell lines to identify lineage-, genotype-, region-, or cancer-type-specific genes required for proliferation or survival, including synthetic-lethal vulnerabilities and candidate therapeutic dependencies.

Used COLT-Cancer essentiality measurements to benchmark or evaluate dependency-prediction, shRNA off-target correction, gene-solution inference, cross-site reproducibility, coessentiality, and comparisons with CRISPR screens.

Used filtered essential-gene or essential-protein targets from specified cancer cell lines and networks to construct network-controllability models, select driver proteins, and evaluate drug-target-aware control or multi-drug therapy strategies.
Used essentiality annotations in broader analyses of protein age versus human PPI-network essentiality and in resources assessing epigenetic- and apoptosis-gene essentiality.

name: TCGA-LGG
descriptions: Engrailed 1 overexpression as a potential prognostic marker in Lower Grade Glioma.
usage_summaries: Researchers used lower-grade glioma transcriptomic and clinical data to define molecular subtypes, develop prognostic signatures and assess individual gene biomarkers, sometimes validating findings in external cohorts.
They stratified expression and clinical data by age, grade, sex, IDH status and 1p/19q codeletion to investigate prognosis and glioma progression mechanisms.
Researchers integrated tumour mutation, expression and regulatory-network data to identify glioblastoma driver pathways and potential therapeutic regulatory axes.
usage_patterns: TCGA-LGG transcriptomic and clinical data were used to identify pyroptosis-related genes, define molecular subtypes, and develop prognostic risk signatures for lower-grade glioma, with survival discrimination assessed in TCGA and, for one signature, immunotherapy-response relevance evaluated and external validation performed in CGGA.

TCGA lower-grade glioma expression profiles were compared between younger and older patients to investigate age-related prognosis and differences in cancer, nucleotide-synthesis, mTOR, DNA-repair, mitosis-kinase, and tumor-inflammation programs.

TCGA mutation, expression, and regulatory-network data were integrated to identify phenotypically impactful glioblastoma driver pathways and therapeutic regulatory axes involving TP53, CDKN2A, MDM2, RB1, angiogenesis, apoptosis, proliferation, and PI3K-Akt signaling.

TCGA-derived LGG data were used to evaluate individual gene biomarkers: high BIRC5 or GPX1 expression was associated with poor prognosis, with BIRC5 additionally examined in relation to TP53 mutation and immune-cell infiltration.

TCGA-LGG transcriptomic and clinical data were stratified by grade, sex, IDH status, and 1p/19q codeletion to identify gender- and grade-specific mechanisms of grade 2/3 glioma progression and steroid-signaling prognostic markers, with CGGA cohorts used for validation.

name: ASTRA
descriptions: ASTRA: A Comprehensive Resource of Stress-Induced Transcriptional Activation
usage_patterns: Used to compare differentially expressed genes in treated and irradiated osteosarcoma cells with curated oxidative-stress, DNA-damage, heat-shock, and hypoxia response patterns, helping interpret apoptosis, invasion, and NRF2-related radioresistance findings.

Used with GEO data and structured stress-modality metadata to stratify heterogeneous transcriptomic samples and prioritize stress-associated lncRNAs, enabling comparison of modality-specific and shared transcriptional programs.

name: iUUCD
descriptions: Integrated Ubiquitin and ubiquitin-like conjugation database

The ubiquitin and ubiquitin-like (Ub/Ubl) conjugation is one of the most important post-translational modifications (PTMs) in proteins, and regulates a large number of cellular processes,such as cell cycle, signal transduction, apoptosis and autophagy, while aberrant modification isimplicated in numerous pathologies, such as neurodegenerative disorders, inflammatory diseasesand cancers. Identification and annotation of regulators in Ub/Ubl systems is fundamental forunderstanding the molecular mechanisms of Ub/Ubl conjugations, and provides a highly usefulreservoir for discovering disease biomarkers and drug targets.In 2013, we reported a family-based database of UUCD 1.0 for ubiquitin and ubiquitin-likeconjugations, containing 738 ubiquitin-activating enzyme (E1s), 2,937 ubiquitin-conjugatingenzymes (E2s), 46,631 ubiquitin-protein ligases (E3s) and 6,647 deubiquitinating enzymes(DUBs) in 70 eukaryotes (1), whereas proteins with ubiquitin domains (UBDs) and ubiquitin-likedomains (ULDs) were not included at that time (2,3). In this update, we greatly improved ourprevious database, and provided a much more comprehensive resource of iUUCD 2.0(http://iuucd.biocuckoo.org/). Firstly, 27 E1s, 109 E2s, 1,153 E3s, 164 DUBs, 396 UBDs and 183ULDs were collected from scientific literatures and classified into 1, 4, 23, 8, 27, 11 families,respectively. Secondly, HMM identification and ortholog search were adopted to detect thepotential regulators. Ultimately, the iUUCD 2.0 totally contains 136,512 regulators in ubiquitin andubiquitin-like conjugation systems, including 1,230 E1s, 5,636 E2s, 93,343 E3s, 9,548 DUBs,30,173 UBDs and 11,099 ULDs in 148 eukaryotic species. In particular, we provided richannotations for regulators of eight model organisms, especially in humans, by compiling andintegrating the knowledge from nearly 70 widely used public databases that cover (i) CancerMutations, including ICGC, COSMIC, TCGA, CGAP and IntOGen; (ii) Single NucleotidePolymorphisms (SNPs), such as dbSNP; (iii) mRNA Expression, including GEO, ArrayExpress,GXD, FFGED, TCGA, ICGC, COSMIC, HUMAN PROTEOME MAP and The Human Protein Atlas;(iv) DNA and RNA Elements, including UTRdb, AREsite, JASPAR CORE, circBase, circRNADb,CircNet, Circ2Traits, miRTarBase, microRNA.org, TRANSFAC, miRWalk, TargetScan, miRecords,RepTar, miRNAMap, SomamiR DB 2.0, miRcode, RAID v2.0 and LncRNADisease; (v) Protein-protein Interactions (PPIs), including IID, iRefIndex, PINA, HINT, Mentha, SZDB and InWeb_IM;(vi) Protein 3D Structures, including PDB, MMDB and SCOP; (vii) Disease-associated information,including ClinVar, OMIM, GWASdb and GWAS CENTRAL; (viii) Drug-target Relations, includingDrugBank, TTD, KPID, CARLSBAD, SuperTarget, GRAC and PDTD; (ix) Post-translationalModifications (PTMs), including CPLM, dbPAF, dbPPT, phosSNP, PhosphositePlus,Phospho.ELM, dbPTM, PHOSIDA, BioGRID, HPRD, UniProt, O-GlycBase, PhosphoBase andmUbiSiDa; (x) DNA Methylation, including MethyCancer, TCGA, ICGC and COSMIC; (xi) ProteinExpression/Proteomics, including The Human Protein Atlas, Human Proteome Map and GPMDB.Compared with our previously developed UUCD 1.0 (~0.41 GB), iUUCD 2.0 has a size of ~32.1GB of data with a > 75-fold increase in data volume. We expect that iUUCD 2.0 can be moreuseful for further study of ubiquitin and ubiquitin-like conjugations.
usage_patterns: Defined ubiquitination-related gene sets, including E1, E2, E3, deubiquitinase, binding-domain, and other ubiquitin-system components, for differential-expression, co-expression, enrichment, interaction-network, and downstream gene analyses in cancer, infection, myopia, and other disease studies.

Provided ubiquitination-related genes for molecular subtyping, prognostic or risk-signature construction, and clinical, immune-infiltration, drug-sensitivity, or survival analyses across cervical, liver, ovarian, breast, endometrial, colorectal, renal, lung, thyroid, gastric, melanoma, sepsis, sarcoma, and other cancers.

Supplied E3-ligase or ubiquitin-system memberships for experimental target selection, including defining an E3-cDNA or CRISPR screening library, screening autophagy regulators, and compiling candidates for degrader or PROTAC development.

Supplied ubiquitin-system protein sequences or annotations for proteomics identification, candidate-ligase prioritization, substrate discovery, ubiquitin-binding-protein filtering, and interpretation of MHC class I peptide changes after UPS-pathway inhibition.

Provided HMM profiles or family annotations to identify ubiquitin and ubiquitin-like pathway genes in plant genomes and other species, including Gastrodia, Dendrobium, Lonicera, Rosa, and Catharanthus, and to compare conserved versus lineage-specific E3 ligases.

Contributed curated ubiquitin-related gene families or enzyme annotations to integrated annotation, search, and multi-omics resources, including PlantGSAD, DOO, IC4R, BIG Search, and RNA-binding E3-ligase catalogs.
Provided a curated proteostasis or ubiquitin-system gene set used as a benchmark for transcriptomic effects of H2BK17A under ad libitum and time-restricted feeding in Drosophila.
Supplied annotations for human ubiquitin-like domain-containing proteins used in sequence filtering and alignment to identify representative domains and candidate RNA-binding proteins.

Contributed ubiquitin-system or E3-ligase annotations to method or resource evaluation, including classification of E3-specific ubiquitination sites and quantitative characterization of ubiquitination regulatory networks.

name: ApInAPDB
descriptions: A database of apoptosis-inducing anticancer peptides.
usage_summaries: Researchers used ApInAPDB Bim BH3 peptide structures to design and screen more helical Mcl-1-targeting analogues. They docked literature-derived peptides and evaluated candidate complexes through bioinformatics and molecular-dynamics simulations, including comparison with Bcl-XL.
usage_patterns: Used to identify a lead BIM-derived peptide sequence for designing more helical analogues targeting the anti-apoptotic protein Mcl-1, followed by bioinformatics and molecular-dynamics evaluation.

Supplied tertiary structures of literature-derived Bim BH3 peptides for docking and molecular-dynamics screening against Mcl-1, identifying E2gI and E2gY as stable high-affinity candidates relative to Bcl-XL.

name: LncTarD: a manually-curated database of experimentally-supported functional lncRNAÃ¢â‚¬â€œtarget regulations in human diseases
usage_summaries: Researchers used experimentally supported lncRNA–target regulation to interpret disease-related expression, copy-number and variant analyses, and to prioritise regulatory candidates for experimental follow-up. These studies covered paediatric cancer with birth defects, depression, pituitary adenomas, osteoarthritis, spermatogenesis and lung adenocarcinoma.

Researchers incorporated supported lncRNA interactions into functional-enrichment and regulatory-network analyses, including competing endogenous RNA networks. They also contributed these interactions, mechanisms and contextual evidence to integrated human and mouse annotation and interactome resources.

Researchers constructed lncRNA–protein and lncRNA–gene prediction benchmarks from supported interactions, testing generalisation under sequence- and protein-grouped splits. One benchmark used positive lncRNA–gene pairs with matched random negatives.
usage_patterns: Mapped lncRNAs affected by copy-number variants in pediatric birth-defect cancer patients to experimentally supported targets and regulators, then examined enrichment in cancer growth, cancer-pathway, and apoptosis functions.
Predicted lncRNAs associated with VEGFα and PTEN in a mouse depression brain–gut-axis study and selected candidates using target overlap and tissue-expression evidence.

Identified experimentally reported lncRNAs regulating EGFR and STAT3 during biomarker discovery for non-functioning pituitary adenomas, then filtered candidates by redundancy and normal-pituitary expression correlation for experimental follow-up.
Combined LncTarD interactions with other resources to construct lncRNA–protein interaction datasets and assess prediction generalization under sequence- and protein-grouped train/test splits.
Added LncTarD-supported lncRNA–mRNA interactions to a differential-expression-based lncRNA–miRNA–mRNA competing endogenous RNA network, followed by correlation and pathway-enrichment analysis.
Built an independent positive-pair benchmark from LncTarD, with 192 positive lncRNA–gene pairs and matched random negatives, to train and compare relationship-prediction models.

Searched experimentally supported lncRNA regulation to interpret genes shared across bulk and single-cell knee-osteoarthritis analyses, identifying CYTOR–NRP1 regulation involving miR-206 as a database-supported mechanism.

Supplied experimentally supported lncRNA–target interactions, including lncRNA–mRNA, lncRNA–protein, and lncRNA–miRNA links classified by validation strength, for RNAenrich’s ncRNA functional-enrichment mapping.
Contributed experimentally supported lncRNA–target regulations and regulatory mechanisms to integrated human and mouse cancer lncRNA annotations in NONCODEV6.

Contributed experimentally validated RNA–protein and RNA–RNA interactions, together with contextual evidence such as tissues, cell lines, and target regions, to the integrated RNAInter v4.0 interactome.

Provided curated lncRNA annotations and interacting-partner evidence used with other resources to functionally annotate TUG1 and distinguish experimentally validated from predicted associations in LncRNAWiki 2.0.
Contributed regulatory relationships to RegNetwork 2025’s integrated, confidence-scored human and mouse network of TF, miRNA, lncRNA, circRNA, and gene interactions.
Used experimentally supported lncRNA–target links to identify disease-specific regulatory candidates relevant to spermatogenesis, including TAZ, LIN28A, CDKN-family genes, EZH2, SUZ12, and VEGFA.
Retrieved documented disease-associated functions of host lncRNAs to test whether functional annotation was associated with positive expression coupling between embedded snoRNAs and their host genes.
Mapped variants located in non-coding RNA regions to database-supported targets during whole-genome variant interpretation.
Queried supported lncRNA interactions for starvation-induced lncRNAs in lung adenocarcinoma cells, testing links to EZH2 and FTO and comparing database evidence with literature and RT-PCR validation.

Combined LncTarD with other lncRNA resources to predict disease- and pathway-related regulators, prioritizing TUG1, HOTAIR, MEG3, and H19 as candidates involving CTNNB1, SIRT1, DNMT1, and related pathways.

name: ADPriboDB
descriptions: ADP-ribosylated proteins and sites

ADPriboDB is a database of ADP-ribosylated proteins and their literature-identified ADP-ribosylated residues. The database includes a variety of information for each entry, including any drug treatments performed to obtain the identification of the modification, cell lines and species, the ADP-ribosyltransferases responsible for synthesizing the modification (if known), as well as the site of modification (if identified).

ADPriboDB is a database to facilitate studies in uncovering insights into the mechanisms and biological significance of ADP-ribosylation. ADPriboDB 2.0 serves as a one-stop repository comprising 48 346 entries and 9097 ADP-ribosylated proteins, of which 6708 were newly identified since the original database release.
usage_summaries: Researchers used ADPriboDB annotations to place protein findings in the context of previously reported ADP-ribosylation, ADP-ribose binding and covalent PARylation. They applied these records when studying apoptosis in MIN6 β cells, mutation sites, stem-cell proteomes, chemical-proteomics candidates, vault interactomes, macrodomain proteins and PARP4–hnRNPM interactions in lung adenocarcinoma.
usage_patterns: ADPriboDB was queried to annotate ADP-ribosylated proteins involved in apoptotic signaling in MIN6 β cells during analysis of ARH3-regulated apoptosis.
ADPriboDB PTM annotations were integrated with other resources to assess whether conserved or cancer-associated AKR1C1 mutations affected known ADP-ribosylation sites.
Curated PARP1 and TNKS substrate annotations were used to interpret paired proteome and ubiquitinome changes in primed and PAR-depleted TIRN stem cells, including DUX4-induced conditions.

Known ADP-ribosylation annotations were used to compare experimentally identified protein sets with prior ADP-ribosylome evidence, including chemical-proteomics targets, replication-fork-associated proteins, and Mac1-enriched candidates.
ADPriboDB was used to identify known covalently PARylated macrodomain-containing proteins while testing whether PAR-binding domains direct proteins toward PARP1-mediated covalent PARylation.
Prior ADP-ribose annotations were used to compare wild-type and PARP4-depleted vault interactomes and identify interactome proteins with evidence of ADP-ribose binding or modification.
ADPriboDB was queried to determine whether hnRNPM had previously been reported as ADP-ribosylated while investigating PARP4–hnRNPM interactions and splicing in lung adenocarcinoma.

name: Aphid Genomics Database
descriptions: An aphid genome database.
Genomic database for the pea aphid (Acyrthosiphon pisum)
The Aphid Genome Database's aim is to improve the current pea aphid genome assembly and annotation, and to provide new aphid genome sequences as well as tools for analysis of these genomes.
usage_patterns: Comparative annotation and evolutionary analysis of aphid genes and gene families, including odorant receptors, gustatory receptors, apoptosis-related genes, Wnt genes, BCR peptides, orphan genes, and chemosensory repertoires across multiple aphid species and outgroups.

Reference genome, gene-set, transcript, and protein sequences were used to identify or annotate genes and transcripts through BLAST, manual curation, RNA-seq confirmation, proteomic peptide matching, and transcriptome-to-genome searches, including voltage-gated sodium channels, PAH, and cathepsin B targets.

Pea aphid assemblies and annotations were used as references for genome completeness, chromosome assignment, assembly-error assessment, gene-duplication analysis, and comparison with newly produced or other hemipteran assemblies.
AphidBase genomes and annotations were incorporated into broader comparative-genomics resources and analyses, including InsectBase integration and OrthoDB orthology delineation.

Pea aphid reference annotations and RNA-seq data supported tissue- or lineage-specific expression analyses, including comparisons of reproductive strategies and identification of aphid effector candidates from head, body, and salivary-gland expression.

AphidBase functioned as a repository for assembled aphid sequences, official gene sets, transcripts, microRNAs, mitochondrial genomes, and other genome-annotation data used in comparative genomics and invasion-related research.
AphidBase was identified as a genome database or public source in reviews and resource descriptions, without a dataset-specific observed analysis.

name: CancerSCEM
descriptions: CancerSCEM: A database of single-cell expression map across various human cancers
Database of single-cell expression map across various human cancers.
usage_patterns: Used CancerSCEM single-cell profiles to characterize gene expression, cell-type localization, and tumor-microenvironment biology across cancers, including RPL7L1 associations with inflammation, hypoxia, and apoptosis; CDK1 and neurotrophic-factor expression across tumor types; and a pan-cancer PLK1-related gene set.

Used cancer-specific CancerSCEM cohorts to investigate candidate biomarkers and mechanisms by measuring gene expression in defined malignant, immune, stromal, or epithelial populations, including KRT7 in PDAC, FGF19 in colorectal cancer, CD276 in glioblastoma, FGL1 in NSCLC, VCX2 in HCC, AURKA/EZH2 in ovarian carcinoma, CDK1/CXCL8 in lung adenocarcinoma, MEG3 in anaplastic thyroid cancer, ORMDL2 in glioblastoma, and MMP12 in LUSC.

Used CancerSCEM as a source of annotated single-cell data for computational method evaluation or validation, including Cancer-Finder malignant-cell annotation against database percentages and a glioblastoma deep-learning resource.

Downloaded and integrated CancerSCEM datasets across cancer types for cross-cancer single-cell analysis, including filtering, Harmony correction, cell-type classification, recurrent malignant-cell programs, and context-dependent expression and cell-cycle patterns.

Reused CancerSCEM datasets to construct larger cancer single-cell resources: SCAR standardized pan-cancer workflows, scDrugAct curated expression matrices for tumor heterogeneity, drug action, and resistance, and TE-SCALE assembled a pan-cancer transposable-element resource from CancerSCEM raw reads.

Used a CancerSCEM lung adenocarcinoma dataset for cell-type annotation and CellChat analysis of intercellular signaling, identifying fibroblasts as major senders and FN1/CXCL pathways as predominant outgoing signals.

name: TRICON8
descriptions:
Collection of samples and data across the following diseases: Malignant tumour of ovary TRICON8 is the translational research sub-study of the ICON8 trial. Its aim is to establish a large, comprehensive biobank comprising tumour tissue, blood and serial plasma samples with associated clinical data which will be an invaluable resource for high-quality translational research in ovarian cancer. 
ICON8 is a phase III randomised controlled trial designed to investigate the safety and efficacy of two dose-dense, dose-fractionated, weekly carboplatin-paclitaxel combination chemotherapy regimens for the treatment of newly diagnosed ovarian cancer compared to standard three-weekly carboplatin-paclitaxel. There is a growing body of evidence that using dose-fractionated paclitaxel in particular may have increased anti-tumour effects, and this is thought to be due to enhanced anti-angiogenic and pro-apoptotic effects.

name: Cell Tracer
descriptions: A database to dissect the causative multilevel interplay contributing to cell development trajectories.
CellTracer: A comprehensive database to dissect causative multi-omics interplay contributing to cellular development trajectory
usage_summaries: Researchers used Cell Tracer single-cell trajectories to relate gene expression to malignant-cell functional states. Across melanoma, hepatocellular, lung and breast cancer datasets, they examined expression along differentiation and pseudo-time trajectories alongside cell-cycle, invasion, proliferation, hypoxia, quiescence, inflammatory and epithelial–mesenchymal-transition states.
usage_patterns: Analyzed TIMM9 expression along single-cell pseudo-time trajectories in malignant cells to relate persistent expression to differentiation, cell-cycle, DNA-repair, proliferation, and invasion phenotypes.

Profiled UBE2S across SKCM single-cell subpopulations, differentiation states, and pseudo-time trajectories, relating its expression to dormancy, invasion, hypoxia, DNA damage, stemness, metastasis, epithelial–mesenchymal transition, proliferation, cell-cycle progression, apoptosis, and quiescence.

Related MYBL2 expression to functional cell states along HCC-associated single-cell trajectories, finding positive association with cell-cycle scores and negative association with inflammation scores.
Examined CEP55-associated processes in lung-cancer single-cell RNA-sequencing data, linking overexpression to invasion, proliferation, metastasis, and epithelial–mesenchymal transition.
Examined EZH2 in breast-cancer cell-development pathways, using CellTracer to associate expression with quiescence, invasion, and hypoxia but not apoptosis.

name: lnc2cancer
descriptions:
An updated resource for experimentally supported lncRNA/circRNA cancer associations and web tools based on RNA-seq and scRNA-seq data.

lncRNA and cancer association database.

Lnc2Cancer, is a manually curated database that provides comprehensive experimentally supported associations between lncRNA or circRNA and human cancer.

Lnc2Cancer 3.0 includes comprehensive data on experimentally supported long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) and circular RNAs (circRNAs) associated with human cancers. In addition, web tools for analyzing lncRNA expression by high-throughput RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) and single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) are described. Lnc2Cancer 3.0 was updated with several new features, including (i) Increased cancer-associated lncRNA entries over the previous version. The current release includes 9254 lncRNA-cancer associations, with 2659 lncRNAs and 216 cancer subtypes. (ii) Newly adding 1049 experimentally supported circRNA-cancer associations, with 743 circRNAs and 70 cancer subtypes. (iii) Experimentally supported regulatory mechanisms of cancer-related lncRNAs and circRNAs, involving microRNAs, transcription factors (TF), genetic variants, methylation and enhancers were included. (iv) Appending experimentally supported biological functions of cancer-related lncRNAs and circRNAs including cell growth, apoptosis, autophagy, epithelial mesenchymal transformation (EMT), immunity and coding ability. (v) Experimentally supported clinical relevance of cancer-related lncRNAs and circRNAs in metastasis, recurrence, circulation, drug resistance, and prognosis was included. Additionally, two flexible online tools, including RNA-seq and scRNA-seq web tools, were developed to enable fast and customizable analysis and visualization of lncRNAs in cancers. Lnc2Cancer 3.0 is a valuable resource for elucidating the associations between lncRNA, circRNA and cancer.
usage_patterns: Served as a curated reference or gold-standard set for evaluating cancer-lncRNA, lncRNA–disease, and lncRNA-candidate prediction methods through enrichment tests, ROC analysis, cross-validation, generalization testing, or benchmark construction.

Provided known cancer-associated lncRNAs or lncRNA–cancer associations for validating predicted disease or cancer relationships, ranking candidates, and assessing cancer-driver, immune-regulatory, or pathophysiological relevance.

Supplied cancer-dysregulated or cancer-associated lncRNAs for downstream molecular and clinical analyses, including ovarian-cancer G-quadruplex screening, endometrial-cancer IGF2BP3 candidates, colorectal-cancer sequence and G-quadruplex analysis, rectal-cancer analysis, LUAD prognosis, pan-cancer stage associations, and circRNA host-gene enrichment.

Contributed curated lncRNA–disease or cancer-related records to integrated knowledge bases, reference collections, single-cell expression resources, disease-enrichment sets, and cancer-only association datasets.
Was used as a comparator when assessing the coverage and inclusion criteria of cancer-lncRNA databases after harmonization to common gene annotations.
Provided cancer-associated lncRNA and circRNA records for constructing a cancer-focused association dataset containing experimentally supported disease relationships.

name: LncSEA
descriptions:
A platform for long non-coding RNA related sets and enrichment analysis.

Welcome to LncSEA a comprehensive human lncRNA sets resource and enrichment analysis platform.
LncSEA 2.0: an updated platform for long non-coding RNA related sets and enrichment analysis
Reference human lncRNA sets
usage_patterns: Functional and regulatory enrichment of lncRNA sets to characterize biological processes, pathways, regulatory factors, interactions, subcellular localization, or disease relevance in cancer and other disease contexts, including NSCLC, DLBCL, ovarian cancer, breast cancer, bladder cancer, cervical cancer, prostate cancer, colorectal cancer, lung adenocarcinoma, and gestational diabetes.

Annotation and enrichment of lncRNAs or lncRNA-derived modules to interpret cancer phenotypes, prognostic signatures, treatment resistance, metastasis, proliferation, invasion, EMT, apoptosis, migration, or patient outcome.

Use of LncSEA regulatory and interaction annotations to construct or interpret lncRNA–mRNA, lncRNA–miRNA, ceRNA, RNA–protein, or target-gene networks, including prediction of candidate regulators and binding partners.
Drug–lncRNA annotation or enrichment to relate predicted, differentially expressed, or prognostic lncRNAs to anticancer drugs and resistance-associated treatment mechanisms.

Use of LncSEA experimentally supported or reference functional sets to validate, expand, or biologically interpret lncRNA candidates and signatures, including cancer-associated lncRNA lists and experimentally validated pathological functions.
Analysis of lncRNA regulation by transcription factors, RNA-binding proteins, chromatin features, or epigenetic marks in aging, osteoarthritis, vaccination, and other transcriptomic contexts.
Assessment of lncRNA co-expression or correlation patterns against disease, culture, or patient datasets to compare model systems with human cancer data.
Use of LncSEA as a general lncRNA annotation and enrichment resource, including comparison with other enrichment tools and examination of the size and composition of its reference gene sets.

name: microRNA.org
descriptions: microRNA target predictions and expression profiles
usage_patterns: Used with other miRNA target-prediction resources to identify candidate miRNA–mRNA interactions in disease, development, stress, cancer, exercise, and apoptosis-related studies; overlapping predictions were then selected for experimental validation or downstream biological interpretation.

Used to generate predicted miRNA–gene relationships for regulatory-network construction or cancer-omics querying, including ceRNA networks, integrated regulatory databases, and a portal combining target predictions with expression and survival data.
Used to test the relationship between miRNA-binding sites and transcript features by comparing microRNA.org target sites with m5C locations in 3′ UTRs and evaluating overlap statistically.

name: Reactome
descriptions: Database of human biological pathways and processes ranging from basic processes of metabolism to complex regulatory pathways. The data is curated by biologists and subsequently peer-reviewed for accuracy and consistency. Cross-references with UniProt, PubMed, Ensembl, Gene Ontology and LocusLink are also provided. It supersedes The Genome Knowledgebase project.

Reactome is a curated database of biological processes in humans. It covers biological pathways ranging from the basic processes of metabolism to high-level processes such as hormonal signalling. While Reactome is targeted at human pathways, it also includes many individual biochemical reactions from non-human systems such as rat, mouse, fugu fish and zebra fish. This makes the database relevant to the large number of researchers who work on model organisms. All the information in Reactome is backed up by its provenance: either a literature citation or an electronic inference based on sequence similarity. Our ontology ensures that the various events are linked in an appropriate spatial and temporal context.The basic information in Reactome is provided by bench biologists who are experts in that domain of biology. The information is then managed and edited by the Reactome staff at CSHL and the EBI, and entered into a relational database. They are then reviewed by other biological researchers for consistency and accuracy. Following peer-review, the information is published to the web.Reactome supersedes an earlier project called The Genome Knowledgebase and incorporates all the information previously available in its predecessor. Reactome sports a radically redesigned user interface in which the entire set of human pathways known to the database are represented as a series of constellations in a "starry sky." The starry sky can be used to navigate through the universe of human reactions and is invaluable to visualize connections between pathways, some of which will be surprising to biologists who are not familiar with pathways outside their domain of research.

Reactome is a manually curated, peer-reviewed pathway database, annotated by expert biologists and cross-referenced to bioinformatics databases. Its aim is to share information in the visual representations of biological pathways in a computationally accessible format. Pathway annotations are authored by expert biologists, in collaboration with Reactome editorial staff and cross-referenced to many bioinformatics databases. These include NCBI Gene, Ensembl and UniProt databases, the UCSC and HapMap Genome Browsers, the KEGG Compound and ChEBI small molecule databases, PubMed, and Gene Ontology.

The cornerstone of Reactome is a freely available, open source relational database of signaling and metabolic molecules and their relations organized into biological pathways and processes. The core unit of the Reactome data model is the reaction. Entities (nucleic acids, proteins, complexes, vaccines, anti-cancer therapeutics and small molecules) participating in reactions form a network of biological interactions and are grouped into pathways. Examples of biological pathways in Reactome include classical intermediary metabolism, signaling, transcriptional regulation, apoptosis and disease. Inferred orthologous reactions are available for 15 non-human species including mouse, rat, chicken, zebrafish, worm, fly, and yeast.

The Reactome Knowledgebase (https://reactome.org) provides molecular details of signal transduction, transport, DNA replication, metabolism, and other cellular processes as an ordered network of molecular transformationsÃ¢â‚¬â€\x9Dan extended version of a classic metabolic map, in a single consistent data model. Reactome functions both as an archive of biological processes and as a tool for discovering unexpected functional relationships in data such as gene expression profiles or somatic mutation catalogues from tumor cells. To support the continued brisk growth in the size and complexity of Reactome, we have implemented a graph database, improved performance of data analysis tools, and designed new data structures and strategies to boost diagram viewer performance. To make our website more accessible to human users, we have improved pathway display and navigation by implementing interactive Enhanced High Level Diagrams (EHLDs) with an associated icon library, and subpathway highlighting and zooming, in a simplified and reorganized web site with adaptive design. To encourage re-use of our content, we have enabled export of pathway diagrams as Ã¢â‚¬ËœPowerPointÃ¢â‚¬â„¢ files.
The Reactome Pathway Knowledgebase 2022
usage_patterns: Used for pathway enrichment or gene-set analysis of differential-expression results to characterize disease, treatment, cell-state, tissue, and developmental programs across transcriptomic studies, including myeloma, breast cancer, amyloidosis, glomeruli, sensory neurons, senescence, sepsis, cancer, infection, diabetes, neurodegeneration, and immune conditions.

Used for pathway enrichment and functional interpretation of proteomic or protein-list data, including tissue clusters, amyloid-related clusters, acetylated proteins, infection outcomes, cancer subtypes, extracellular vesicles, disease biomarkers, and treatment-associated proteins.

Used to interpret lipidomic, metabolomic, or metabolic-network changes by mapping altered metabolites or reactions to pathways and subnetworks, including viral-transformation lipidomics, polymer-exposure metabolomics, SGLT2 inhibition, and metabolite-annotation expansion.

Provided pathway gene sets or annotations for GWAS, post-GWAS, and variant analyses to prioritize genes, identify disease- or trait-associated pathways, construct evaluation sets, or interpret inherited variation in diabetes, height, adiposity, atrial fibrillation, epilepsy, longevity, and related traits.

Supported single-cell, spatial, chromatin-accessibility, and perturbation analyses by annotating clusters, identifying compartment- or region-specific programs, characterizing outliers, and interpreting cell-type or perturbation responses.

Supplied curated pathway definitions for signatures, pathway scores, and biological filters, including fetal-colon progenitor signatures, HRR and senescence gene sets, metabolic modules, drug-action pathways, and cross-species pathway scores.

Provided pathway priors or structured pathway knowledge for network, machine-learning, and causal analyses, including drug–disease proximity, multiplex embeddings, protein-interaction models, pathway-constrained multi-omics encoders, and hypergraph shortest-path computation.

Supplied curated pathway and interaction content for biomedical databases, browsers, and analysis platforms, including STRING, CTD, Monarch, PANGEA, g:Profiler, Enrichr-KG, KOBAS, BioMart, PRIDE, Complex Portal, Alliance, Ensembl, and pathway-visualization tools.

Provided curated pathway annotations for disease, chemical, gene, protein-complex, and therapeutic-target integration, supporting functional annotation, mechanistic inference, network construction, and hypothesis generation.

Was used as a pathway resource in method evaluation, including comparisons of enrichment stability, pathway-scoring accuracy, annotation coverage, and the effects of gene-set choice or background selection.
Supported pathway visualization and interactive exploration by supplying curated pathway models, reaction networks, and pathway overlays for gene or protein datasets.

Provided pathway content for integrating or extending specialized resources, including lipid-reaction incorporation into LIPID MAPS, disease-term mapping, toxicogenomics, protein-complex cross-references, and community-curation workflows.
Supplied curated human pathway models for cross-species or non-human functional annotation, including model-organism gene sets, canine transcriptomic analysis, and projected C. elegans pathways.

Provided pathway information for therapeutic or drug-target analyses, including drug-mechanism proximity, immune-target selection, compound validation, and pathway-based links between type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer’s disease.

name: ORFDB
descriptions: A major challenge following the sequencing of the human genome is to determine the biological functions of the estimated 30,000 genes. This requires the biochemical characterization of expressed proteins in various hosts. To facilitate the protein expression in a high throughput fashion, Invitrogen initiated an ORFeome program about one and half years ago. This ORFeome program is intended to provide the Open Reading Frames (ORFs) of all human proteins to researchers in academics and government, biotech and pharmaceutical industries. Each ORF was PCR-amplified using gene specific primer set from cDNA clone or library and the amplified DNA fragment was cloned into Gateway entry vector using recombination based cloning in a high throughput format. The positive ORF clone was then subject to full-insert sequence verification. The qualified ORF clones are guaranteed to match 100% to public protein sequence. Last December, we launched a web based ORFBrowser to allow users to query our ORFeome database. The ORFBrowser provides not only standard query tools like blast and keyword search, but also advanced browse by Gene Ontology, and a fast and flexible ID search in a batch mode. Using GO Browser, users can easily browse through the ORF collections based on biological processes, cellular component, and molecular function. Using the ID search, the user can query ORFeome database using the IDs such as Unigene ID, LocusLinkID, Gene Symbol, gene accession number and protein accession number or the combination of these IDs, in a batch mode with up to 10,000 IDs in a single query. In addition, Each ORF has been annotated extensively and the annotation of each ORF is captured in the ORFCard, which is summarized in six categories: Gene, ORF, Clone, Protein, SNP and Genomic links. 1. Gene information contains the gene definition, function annotation, related accessions, gene symbol, GO classification, links for CGAP gene expression profile and PubMed references. 2. ORF information contains the ORF size, nucleotide and protein sequences as well as Phred quality values for each base of the ORF. 3. Clone information has the vector type, host cell and clone collection. 4. Protein annotation includes the basic feature of the protein, function annotation, related accessions, protease digestion profile, disease link with OMIM id, secondary structure prediction as well as the links to map the protein to well-known protein domain mapping sites like, PFAM, Prosite, SMART and link to map the protein to SwissModel 5. SNP information contains the links to NCBI SNP database. 6. Genomic Links include links to Unigene, LocusLink, Ensembl, MGI, as well as the link to map the protein to Human genomic backbone using online UCSC Blat tool.  With this ORFCard, the users can easily access the most current information for the ORF of interest in various categories with their finger click. The access of this information is absolutely free of charge to anyone and the user has no obligation to buy the ORF clones.  Currently, the ORFeome database has 4500 human ORFs and 2800 mouse ORFs. We will be releasing 2000 clones every three months. To our knowledge, ORFeome database provides the largest ORF collection for human and mouse Open Reading Frames and these ORF clones will facilitate the function dissection of individual proteins.
usage_summaries: Researchers used human full-length ORF clones to construct a proteome microarray, producing and purifying thousands of proteins for high-throughput protein-affinity studies.
They also used human ORF clones in Gateway-based yeast two-hybrid screens of apoptosis-related protein interactions in breast cancer, followed by functional validation of selected interactions.
usage_patterns: Supplied human full-length ORF clones for constructing a proteome microarray to produce and purify thousands of proteins for high-throughput protein-affinity studies.
Supplied human ORF clones for Gateway-based yeast two-hybrid screening of apoptosis-related protein interactions in breast cancer, followed by functional validation of selected interactions.

name: Death Domain database
descriptions: A manually curated database of protein-protein interactions for Death Domain Superfamily. The DD superfamily is one of the largest classes of protein interaction modules, and plays a pivotal role in apoptosis, inflammation, necrosis and immune cell signalling pathways.
Protein interaction data for Death Domain superfamily
usage_summaries: Researchers used the Death Domain Database to identify a putative death-domain region in Drosophila Relish and compare it with the mammalian NF-κB1 p105 death domain. This informed investigation of a possible Relish–dRYBP interaction while assessing rare protein-altering variants in inflammasome-regulatory genes in multiple sclerosis.
usage_patterns: To investigate whether rare protein-altering variants in inflammasome-regulatory genes contribute to multiple sclerosis, researchers used the Death Domain Database to identify a putative death-domain region in Drosophila Relish and compare it with the mammalian NF-κB1 p105 death domain as evidence for a possible Relish–dRYBP interaction.
